<meta>continues from previous page: the soul, for even in the Nymphae-</meta>
<warning>The left margin of the page is tightly cropped, resulting in the loss of letters at the beginning of several lines. These have been restored based on the context of the Latin text.</warning>
an pool, certain islands proceeding from the mainland, moved in a circle,
lead a dance <note>original: "choream ducunt"</note>, then return to the shores. Marcus Varro
testifies that he saw them. And there are things more wonderful than these: for on the Attic
shore the sea sounds like a lyre <term>citharam</term>. At Megara a certain rock,
at every stroke <note>restored from "ad singulos ictus"</note>, plays like a lute, so great is the power of Music. It
indeed <note>restored from "quidem"</note> soothes the soul, lifts the mind, incites warriors to
war, and relieves the labors and exhaustion of individual works.
It restores those who have fallen and are desperate, and comforts travelers.
And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted
by their singing drivers. In the same way, those carrying heavy
burdens sing, and are made capable and relieved by it: for singing
produces delight and aptitude; it softens the wrathful,
gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant,
tempers the madness of the frenzied, and dissipates vain thoughts:
hence it is that certain diseases of the body and soul can be
either cured or induced in this way, as Democritus and Theophrastus
affirm. So we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna <note>Arion was a legendary Greek kitharode, a performer on the lyre.</note>

<summary>This page describes the miraculous and psychological effects of music, citing examples of musical rocks and islands, and how melody can comfort laborers, soothe animals, and heal diseases of the mind.</summary>
<keywords>music, harmony, soul, Varro, Arabes, Democritus, Theophrastus, Terpander, Arion, psychological effects, healing</keywords>
